Primates_modeling

Gene Estrada

2023-05-16

Here is the original continuous model (brms3 in the CSCAR rmd file)

brms3 <- brm(ground.use.prop ~
                 Estrada.Continent +                           #continent
                 AvBody.mass.comb.sc +                         #body mass
                 Perc.fruit.comb.sc +                          #percent fruit in diet
                 WC1_area_mean.sc +                            #max temperature (mean across range)
                 WC12_area_mean.sc +                           #rainfall   
                 FH.Median.sc +                                #forest height
                 TC.median.sc +                                #canopy cover percentage
               (1|gr(TenK.tax, cov = A)),
               family = zero_inflated_beta(link = "logit"),
               data = primates,
               data2 = list(A = A),
               iter = 6000, warmup = 2000, thin = 1,
               prior = c(prior(normal(0,10), class = "Intercept"),
                         prior(normal(0,1), class = "b")),
               control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9999),
               cores = 10)

###Female body mass

Here I have ran the same model as above, but used female body mass instead of averaged body mass between males and females. The number of taxa included in the model decreases from 132 in the brms3 model above, to 112

#running continuous model using female body mass instead of av body mass
brms3.1 <- brm(ground.use.prop ~
               Estrada.Continent +                           
               FBody.mass.comb.sc +                         # female body mass
               Perc.fruit.comb.sc +                          
               WC1_area_mean.sc +                            
               WC12_area_mean.sc +                              
               FH.Median.sc +                                
               TC.median.sc +                                
               (1|gr(TenK.tax, cov = A)),
             family = zero_inflated_beta(link = "logit"),
             data = primates,
             data2 = list(A = A),
             iter = 6000, warmup = 2000, thin = 1,
             prior = c(prior(normal(0,10), class = "Intercept"),
                       prior(normal(0,1), class = "b")),
             control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9999),
             cores = 10)

###Home range.

Adding home range as a predictor in the models. Home range and body mass are highly correlated, however:

plot(primates$AvBody.mass.comb.log ~ primates$Redding.Home.range)

cor(primates$AvBody.mass.comb.log, primates$Redding.Home.range, method = "pearson", use = "complete.obs")
## [1] 0.6979416

Adding home range to the model anyway. Multiple error messages pop up. Rhat values are normal but ESS values are low, indicating less reliable coefficient estimates. Probably related to including two highly correlated variables - there doesn’t seem to be any issue with collinearity, however, according to the collinearity check. But looking at the coefficient plot, the estimates look odd. Not sure what to make of this, but moving forward without inlcuding home range for now.

                 Estrada.Continent +                           #continent
                 AvBody.mass.comb.sc +
                 Redding.Home.range +                         #body mass

                 WC1_area_mean.sc +                            #max temperature (mean across range)
                 WC12_area_mean.sc +                           #rainfall   
                 FH.Median.sc +                                #forest height
                 TC.median.sc +                                #canopy cover percentage
               (1|gr(TenK.tax, cov = A)),
               family = zero_inflated_beta(link = "logit"),
               data = primates,
               data2 = list(A = A),
               iter = 6000, warmup = 2000, thin = 1,
               prior = c(prior(normal(0,10), class = "Intercept"),
                         prior(normal(0,1), class = "b")),

###NDVI

Adding NDVI to the models. Running the model after simply adding NDVI resulted in a lot of errors. The collinearity check also showed high VIF values for NDVI and Canopy Cover. Running the model without canopy cover works just fine, though.

brms3.3 <- brm(ground.use.prop ~ 
                 Estrada.Continent +                           #continent
                 AvBody.mass.comb.sc +                         #body mass
                 Perc.fruit.comb.sc +                          #percent fruit in diet
                 WC1_area_mean.sc +                            #max temperature (mean across range)
                 WC12_area_mean.sc +                           #rainfall   
                 FH.Median.sc +                                #forest height
                 NDVI.MED.sc +                                 #median NDVI 
                 (1|gr(TenK.tax, cov = A)),
               family = zero_inflated_beta(link = "logit"),
               data = primates,
               data2 = list(A = A),
               iter = 6000, warmup = 2000, thin = 1,
               prior = c(prior(normal(0,10), class = "Intercept"),
                         prior(normal(0,1), class = "b")),
               control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9999),
               cores = 10)

Predation Pressure

Following Eppley et al. (2022), I created a metric of predation pressure - an integer value representing the number of terrestrial carnivores whose ranges overlap with the focal primate AND with a body mass that is at least 25% of the focal primate’s mass. Carnivore range data from the IUCN, terrestriality data from the PanTHERIA database, and body mass data from the Animal Diversity Web and PanTHERIA databases.

Running the model first with avg body mass

brms3.5 <- brm(ground.use.prop ~ 
                 Estrada.Continent +                           #continent
                 AvBody.mass.comb.sc +                         #body mass
                 Perc.fruit.comb.sc +                          #percent fruit in diet
                 WC1_area_mean.sc +                            #max temperature (mean across range)
                 WC12_area_mean.sc +                           #rainfall   
                 FH.Median.sc +                                #forest height
                 NDVI.MED.sc +                                 #median NDVI
                 n.carn.sc +                                   #number of carnivores (predation pressure proxy)
                 (1|gr(TenK.tax, cov = A)),
               family = zero_inflated_beta(link = "logit"),
               data = primates,
               data2 = list(A = A),
               iter = 6000, warmup = 2000, thin = 1,
               prior = c(prior(normal(0,10), class = "Intercept"),
                         prior(normal(0,1), class = "b")),
               control = list(adapt_delta = 0.9999),
               cores = 10)

##Ancestral State Reconstruction This is still in a work in progress, but so far I’ve been able to visualize the ACR using the {phytools} package

Some prep work first to create a vector that {phytools} can use

#reading in an excel file that I used to align the two different taxonomies used for 10kTrees and IUCN
taxa <- read.csv(file = "10k_primate_tree_taxa.xls.csv", header = TRUE)
colnames(taxa) <- c("X10k_tax", "scientific_name", "remove")
#adding terrestriality data from my 'primates' data set
taxa <- left_join(taxa, primates[,c("scientific_name", "Terrestrial.binary", "Terrestrial.ordinal")], by = "scientific_name")

#reading in the binary tree from 10kTrees
binary_tree <- read.nexus(file = "10kTrees_Primates_binary.nex")

#fixing the Latin binomials first (had to run twice to remove the underscore preceding the subspecies name as well)
binary_tree$tip.label <- sub("_"," ", binary_tree$tip.label)
binary_tree$tip.label <- sub("_"," ", binary_tree$tip.label)

#creating binary terrestriality data frame in structure used by ggtree heat map
terr_bin_data <- data.frame(taxa[taxa$X10k_tax %in% binary_tree$tip.label, 4])
rownames(terr_bin_data) <- taxa[taxa$X10k_tax %in% binary_tree$tip.label, 1]

terr_bin_data <- setNames(terr_bin_data$taxa.taxa.X10k_tax..in..binary_tree.tip.label..4., rownames(terr_bin_data))

I can run some different Ancestral State Reconstruction functions, which take different approaches. It would seem the Bayesian approach would be best, since I’m using Bayesian models above for this data. the fastAnc() function uses Fesenstein’s contrasts algorith (1985) while the anc.Bayes() function uses MCMC to estimate states for all internal nodes of the primate phylogenetic tree

anc_result <- fastAnc(binary_tree, terr_bin_data) 
anc_result

visualizing ACR - the visualization process seems completely separate from the ACR process above, and I’m not sure why. Here I am able to visualize a tree for the binary terrestriality data, inserting points at the nodes where character transitions occur. The ancestral state estimation is done using MCMC

#ancestral state estimation 
simmap_bin <- make.simmap(binary_tree, terr_bin_data, Q = "mcmc")
## Running MCMC burn-in. Please wait....
## Running 100 generations of MCMC, sampling every 100 generations.
## Please wait....
## 
## make.simmap is simulating with a sample of Q from
## the posterior distribution
## 
## Mean Q from the posterior is
## Q =
##              FALSE         TRUE
## FALSE -0.006367248  0.006367248
## TRUE   0.006367248 -0.006367248
## and (mean) root node prior probabilities
## pi =
## FALSE  TRUE 
##   0.5   0.5
## Done.
#plotting
plotSimmap(simmap_bin, 
           lwd = 2, 
           outline = FALSE,
           fsize = 0.3,
           ftype="i",
           ylim = c(-1,Ntip(binary_tree)))
## no colors provided. using the following legend:
##     FALSE      TRUE 
##   "black" "#DF536B"
add.simmap.legend(colors = c("black", "#DF536B"), prompt = FALSE)  #legend text doesn't show up. not sure how to add it
chg <- markChanges(simmap_bin,  plot = FALSE)
points(chg, pch = 16)
